findings.location: exceptions[] (provision absent throughout); reinforced at orientation[2], decision_logic[3], decision_logic[6] and retrieval_prompts[2]
findings.problem: The section never states the express limit M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 21A places on the counseling duty itself: 'Nothing in this section shall be construed to require a pharmacist to provide counseling if the person presenting the prescription declines to accept such offer for counseling.' It also omits the sentence that triggers the statutory counseling duty in the first place ('If an offer to provide counseling is accepted, the pharmacist shall counsel the person presenting the prescription to the extent the pharmacist deems appropriate'). What the section does teach about declination is only the record consequence, and it presents 247 CMR 9.18(4) as an unqualified mandate ('counseling is required on each new drug therapy and on each drug therapy that ... is deemed to be significant'), with decision_logic[3] saying counseling 'is to be provided, whether because the offer was taken up or because 247 CMR 9.18(4) requires it.'
findings.rationale: Declination is squarely inside the scope the section declares for itself: the subtopic begins 'When counseling is owed and to whom' and expressly covers 'the refusal record'. A candidate given a standard Massachusetts fact pattern - new prescription, offer made, patient declines - is left with an unqualified regulatory mandate and no statement of the statute's own answer, which is that s. 21A does not require the pharmacist to counsel. Because the section quotes the neighbouring sentence of the same statutory paragraph (the presumption) almost verbatim, the omission of this one reads as a gap rather than a scope choice, and it risks teaching that counseling remains compulsory after a refusal. The fix is additive - one entry in exceptions and a clause in decision_logic[6] - so the defect is a MINOR_EDIT rather than a rewrite.

findings.location: orientation[2] ('What the counseling contains is then governed by 247 CMR 9.18(5)') and ma_vs_federal[0]
findings.problem: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 21A carries its own eight-item 'may include, but not be limited to' counseling-content list, and its own third-party-payer sentence ('For the purposes of medical assistance and other third party reimbursements or payment programs, any of the above methods, or a combination thereof, shall constitute an acceptable offer to provide counseling'). Neither appears, and orientation[2] attributes the content question to 247 CMR 9.18(5) alone.
findings.rationale: The section declares both 247 CMR 9.18 and s. 21A as its topic, so the statutory content paragraph is inside scope. The practical effect is small: the regulatory list the section does teach is the wider of the two (it adds 'and disposal' to proper storage and 'or adverse reaction' to the missed-dose item), and the section correctly characterises the list as a professional-judgment menu rather than a script, which is the examinable point either way. Low severity; it does not mislead on Massachusetts facts.

findings.problem: The section renders the carve-back on the statutory inpatient exclusion as 'except to the extent required by applicable federal regulations'. The statute is narrower: 'except to the extent required by regulations promulgated by the Federal Health Care Financing Administration pursuant to the provisions of 42 USC 1396r-8.'
findings.rationale: 'Applicable federal regulations' reads as any federal regulation, whereas the statute reserves only regulations made under the Medicaid drug-rebate provision. The substance the section teaches - that the exclusion yields to a federal requirement - is right, and the section correctly contrasts this with the wider formula in 247 CMR 9.18(10). Low severity and not on its own a failure of paraphrase_fidelity, but the exact reservation is worth restoring, particularly since the companion section on drug utilization review states it precisely.

authorities_checked.exact_section: 247 CMR 9.16(7) and (8); 247 CMR 9.04(15) (checked for any further applicability carve-out touching 9.18)
247 CMR 2.00, Definitions (checked: no definition of 'designee', 'counseling' or 'licensee'; 'Certified Pharmacy Technician' and 'Direct Supervision' defined)

results.summary: Every operative proposition in this section was checked word for word against 247 CMR 9.18 as published by the Board of Registration in Pharmacy and against M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 21A, and the reproduction is unusually exact: the 9.18(1) offer duty and its class of actors, the 9.18(2) training duty on the pharmacist, the 9.18(3) bar on a pharmacy technician or other individual counseling any patient, both limbs of the 9.18(4) trigger, the eight lettered items of the 9.18(5) menu including 9.18(5)(h), the three separate 9.18(6) conditions on the consultation area (privacy, 'Patient Consultation Area' signage, and an access route that does not traverse a stockroom or the dispensing area), the 9.18(7) sign at not less than 11 by 14 inches in letters not less than one half inch adjacent to each dispensing area with the prescribed wording, the 9.18(8) availability duty, the 9.18(9) measuring-device duty over all liquid medications, and the 9.18(10) practitioner-keyed carve-out. On the statutory side the offer methods, the needs-or-availability exception, the toll-free pathway with its 'label affixed to each container' placement, the three permitted record locations, and the presumption arising from the absence of any record of a failure to accept were all confirmed verbatim. 247 CMR 8.02(2)(b) and 8.04(4)(b), which let a technician relay the pharmacist's offer to counsel but bar a technician from providing patient counseling, independently corroborate the section's central distinction. All twelve mapped practice questions are answerable from the section and none is contradicted by it. The single substantive defect is an omission: the section never states that s. 21A does not require a pharmacist to counsel a person who declines the offer, even though declination is inside its declared scope and it quotes the adjoining sentence of the same paragraph. Two Low imprecisions accompany it. MINOR_EDIT.

authorities_checked.exact_section: 247 CMR 9.16(7)(a)-(d) and 9.16(8), Maintenance of Pharmacy Records
247 CMR 9.04(15), 9.19(23)-(24), 9.21(11) (swept for any further applicability carve-out reaching 9.16 or 9.17)
247 CMR 2.00, Definitions (checked: no definition of 'medication order', 'patient record' or 'computerized pharmacy system')

results.summary: This section survives a line-by-line comparison with the two provisions it declares. 247 CMR 9.17(1) was confirmed to impose the DUR 'before each new prescription or medication order is dispensed or delivered to a patient or a patient's agent' and then to introduce items (a) through (j) with a permissive 'The DUR may include ... by making a reasonable effort to identify the following'; the section's central teaching point - that the verb governing the list is 'may' while the verb governing the review is 'shall' - is exactly right, and the four items it identifies as present in the regulation but absent from the statute (over- or under-utilization, drug-food interaction, any significant change in drug, dose or directions, and any age related contraindications) check out against both texts. 247 CMR 9.17(2) and its unconditional 'A pharmacist shall document any measures taken in response to a drug utilization review' are reproduced faithfully, as is 9.17(3) with Plumb's Veterinary Drug Handbook at item (d) and 'other peer-reviewed medical literature' at item (e). In 247 CMR 9.16(7) the regulation does state the content duty under a reasonable-effort standard and the immediate-retrieval duty without any qualifier, exactly as the section teaches, and the four lettered profile categories are quoted correctly; 9.16(8) removes institutional sterile compounding pharmacies from the whole of 9.16. The statutory carve-out was verified in its own words, including the reservation for regulations under 42 USC 1396r-8, and I confirmed that 247 CMR 9.17 carries no comparable carve-out and that no other applicability paragraph in 247 CMR 9.00 reaches 9.16 or 9.17. All seven mapped practice questions are answerable from the section and consistent with it. I found nothing wrong. KEEP.

findings.location: orientation[5] ('247 CMR 9.04(8) settles who may take a new prescription over the telephone' and 'The technician limb carries two separate conditions'); exceptions[5] ('247 CMR 9.04(8) states no exception'); decision_logic[4]; role_duties[5]; quick_review[10]
findings.problem: The Board regulates the same activity twice. 247 CMR 8.04(4)(c) provides that a certified pharmacy technician, 'after identifying him or herself as such,' may request refill authorizations and, with the approval of the pharmacist on duty, 'receive new or omitted prescription information from the prescriber or agent, except where otherwise prohibited by federal or state laws and regulations.' The section teaches the technician limb as carrying exactly two conditions (certification and the on-duty pharmacist's approval), states flatly that 9.04(8) 'states no exception', and instructs the reader in decision_logic[4] to hand any new telephoned prescription to an intern or an approved certified technician. The self-identification condition and the express carve-back for other federal and state law are nowhere stated.
findings.rationale: The carve-back is not decorative. For an oral prescription for a controlled substance, M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 20(a) casts the receiving and transcribing role on the pharmacist, and federal law is narrower still for a Schedule II emergency oral prescription. A candidate applying this section to a Massachusetts fact pattern in which a certified technician takes a telephoned controlled-substance prescription would be steered to 'permitted' on the strength of two conditions the section presents as exhaustive. Everything the section says about 247 CMR 9.04(8) read in isolation is accurate - the paragraph does name an intern and an approved certified technician and no one else, and the intern limb does lack the approval qualifier - so the repair is additive: name the self-identification condition and the 'except where otherwise prohibited by federal or state laws and regulations' reservation, and qualify the claim that 9.04(8) 'settles' the question. MINOR_EDIT, not a rewrite.

findings.location: orientation[6], exceptions[6], quick_review[12], decision_logic[5], role_duties[7], retrieval_prompts[10]
findings.problem: The first pamphlet exception is rendered as 'the patient is receiving outpatient palliative care'. M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 21 states it as 'the patient is receiving outpatient palliative care pursuant to section 227 of chapter 111', and the cross-reference is what fixes what counts as palliative care for this purpose.
findings.rationale: Dropping a defining cross-reference loosens an exception that the section otherwise states with care, and a fact pattern could turn on whether the care in question is s. 227 palliative care. The other two exceptions and the trigger itself are quoted exactly, and the section's principal teaching point - that these exceptions belong to the pamphlet and never reach s. 18D - is correct. Low severity; not on its own a failure of paraphrase_fidelity.

authorities_checked.exact_section: 247 CMR 9.04(3), 9.04(7), 9.04(8); and 9.04(15) for the institutional sterile compounding disapplication
105 CMR 700.002(B), (C) and (D) (Massachusetts Schedules II, III and IV adopt 21 CFR 1308.12, .13 and .14)

results.summary: The statutory core of this section is reproduced with real precision. Every element of the M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 21 container label was matched against the statute - date of filling, pharmacy name and address, filling pharmacist's initials, serial number, patient name unless veterinary, prescriber name, name of the controlled substance, directions for use and cautionary statements 'if any, contained in such prescription or required by law', and the tablet or capsule count - and the section is right that the prescriber's registration number is not among them and that a later paragraph extends the labeling provisions beyond controlled substances to drugs dispensed on the prescription of a prescriber registered under section 9. The request-triggered ten-characters-per-inch duty, its attachment to the directions rather than the whole label, and its character as a ceiling on character density are all sound on the statute's words. 247 CMR 9.04(3), 9.04(7) and 9.04(8) were read verbatim and the section's treatment of each is faithful, including the ordered NDC / manufacturer / distributor-packer-repacker fallback and its destination in the computerized pharmacy system, and including the observation that 9.04(15) does not disapply (3), (7) or (8) to institutional sterile compounding pharmacies. M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18D(a) and (b) are quoted essentially word for word and the section is correct that s. 18D states no exception of any kind, so the three s. 21 pamphlet exceptions cannot travel to it. The schedule placements in drug_examples were verified through 105 CMR 700.002, which adopts the federal schedules: buprenorphine is Schedule III and alprazolam Schedule IV. All nine mapped practice questions are answerable from the section and none is contradicted. The one substantive defect is that the section presents the 247 CMR 9.04(8) technician limb as exhaustive while 247 CMR 8.04(4)(c) adds a self-identification condition and an express carve-back for other federal and state law. MINOR_EDIT.
